script.opening: "It’s so embarrassing — I’m bursting for the loo all the time, day and night, and sometimes I just don’t make it. I’ve started avoiding going out and I’m exhausted from getting up at night. Can you just give me a tablet to stop it? My friend takes something for hers."

facts.text: About a year, worse over the last 6 months. A sudden "I have to go NOW" feeling; sometimes leaks on the way, "a proper flood" about twice a week. Goes "every hour or so" in the day. Up 2–3 times a night.
Mostly the rush. If asked: "A little drop if I sneeze hard, but that’s not the problem." Never leaks without knowing.

No blood in the urine ever. No burning, no smelly urine, no fever. No tummy swelling or bloating, no feeling full quickly, no weight loss. No thirst or tiredness. Bowels normal. No back pain or leg numbness. Periods stopped 3 years ago; no bleeding since.
Six or seven mugs of tea and two coffees a day, plus diet cola. "I’ve started drinking less water so I don’t have to go so much." A glass of wine most evenings.

Two children, both normal deliveries (one big baby, 9 lb). No operations. No medicines, no allergies. BMI about 29 ("I’ve put weight on since the menopause"). Not diabetic as far as she knows. Non-smoker.

Works as a school receptionist — can’t leave the desk easily, wears pads. Has stopped going to Zumba and avoids the theatre and long car journeys. Plans routes by where toilets are. Husband is supportive but she feels "old before my time".

Embarrassed and apologetic at first; relax if the doctor normalises it. You want a tablet like your friend’s. If asked to do a bladder diary or bladder training first, be a bit disappointed ("so I can’t have the tablet?") but accept if the doctor explains why and that tablets are still an option later.

ice.ideas: "It’s my age and having the kids. A tablet will stop it — it did for my friend."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — the embarrassment: "I had an accident in Tesco last month. I just left my shopping and went home." She is scared to go anywhere without a toilet nearby and fears smelling of urine at work.
ice.expectations: "The tablet my friend takes." Hasn’t thought about anything other than medicine.

"My friend takes something for hers" — the expectation to negotiate.

checkpoints.text: Recognises OVERACTIVE BLADDER (urgency, frequency, nocturia, urge incontinence) but EXCLUDES other causes/RED FLAGS first — urine infection (dip/culture), diabetes/polyuria, neurological causes, medications — and, as persistent urgency/frequency is a NICE NG12 ovarian symptom, measures CA125 at 40+ (urgent ultrasound at 50–59 if 31 IU/mL or more)

Specifically checks for VISIBLE HAEMATURIA and recognises unexplained visible haematuria at 45+ (without UTI, or persisting/recurring after UTI treatment) as a NICE NG12 red flag for bladder cancer warranting a suspected cancer pathway urology referral
Characterises the incontinence type (urge vs stress vs mixed) with a focused history (± face-to-face examination) and a bladder diary (at least 3 days), as management differs

Follows the CONSERVATIVE-FIRST pathway — bladder diary, lifestyle (reduce caffeine/alcohol, sensible fluids, weight loss), and BLADDER TRAINING for at least 6 weeks (± pelvic floor exercises if stress/mixed) BEFORE medication

Reserves MEDICATION for after conservative measures — antimuscarinic (counselling anticholinergic side-effects and caution in older/frail) reviewed at 4 weeks, or mirabegron (NICE TA290; BP checked, contraindicated at 180/110 or more, MHRA October 2015), vaginal oestrogen if postmenopausal atrophy — and refers to continence/urology if refractory
Acknowledges the significant social/sleep/quality-of-life impact and EMBARRASSMENT, takes it seriously, and frames conservative management positively rather than dismissively
Responds to the "just a pill" request by validating the wish for relief while explaining the conservative-first rationale, and checks understanding

Safety-nets and follows up: red flags warranting review (unexplained visible haematuria → suspected cancer pathway urology referral, persistent urgency/frequency → CA125, infection, neurological symptoms), the bladder-training/diary plan with review, medication as a next step, and continence-service signposting — conservative-first with the NICE NG12 safety-net

worked.txt: "This is really common and nothing to be embarrassed about — and it’s clearly affecting your life, stopping you going out and wrecking your sleep. That matters, and we will sort it. Let me just check a few things first so we treat the right problem."

"A few important checks: any blood in your urine? Any burning or signs of infection? Are you very thirsty or losing weight? Any bloating, feeling full quickly or pelvic pain? … I’ll test your urine, and as the urgency is happening so often, I’d like a blood test called CA125 too. (If haematuria:) Blood in the urine I’d want to investigate urgently with the specialists — not to alarm you, just to be thorough."
"Is it that you get a sudden desperate urge and then leak, or does it leak when you cough or exercise? … Sounds like the urgency type — ‘overactive bladder’. That guides what works best."

"Here’s the thing about tablets — they’re not actually first-line, and the first steps work really well: keeping a bladder diary for at least 3 days, cutting back on caffeine and fizzy drinks (big culprits), and ‘bladder training’ where we gradually stretch the time between visits, for at least 6 weeks. Most people improve a lot with this."

"If that’s not enough after at least 6 weeks, THEN we add a tablet — there are a couple of options, and I’d pick one that suits you, go through the side-effects, check your blood pressure, and review you 4 weeks after starting. So you’re not being denied medication — it’s just the smart order to do things in."

"Start the diary and the caffeine cut, and I’ll show you bladder training; let’s review in a few weeks, and I’d like to see you in person for an examination. Come back sooner if you see any blood in your urine, get burning/fever, or any new numbness or weakness. And there’s continence support if you need products meanwhile."

f.learning: Urinary urgency, frequency, nocturia and urge incontinence suggest OVERACTIVE BLADDER (OAB), but before treating, EXCLUDE other causes and RED FLAGS: urinary infection (urine dip/culture), diabetes/polyuria (glucose/HbA1c), neurological disease, and medications (diuretics, caffeine) — and critically check for unexplained VISIBLE HAEMATURIA (NICE NG12: aged 45 and over without UTI, or persisting/recurring after UTI treatment → suspected cancer pathway urology referral), remembering that persistent urinary urgency or frequency is also an NG12 ovarian cancer symptom (CA125 at 40+; urgent ultrasound at 50–59 if 31 IU/mL or more) — so a pill must not be the first move. Characterise the incontinence type, as management differs: URGE (sudden urgency then leak — OAB), STRESS (leak on cough/exertion — pelvic floor/structural), or MIXED, clarified by a focused history (± face-to-face examination) and a bladder diary. NICE NG123 recommends CONSERVATIVE measures FIRST: a bladder diary (at least 3 days), lifestyle changes (reduce caffeine and alcohol, sensible fluid intake — neither too much nor too little, weight loss if relevant), and BLADDER TRAINING (scheduled voiding with gradually increased intervals for a minimum of 6 weeks), adding pelvic floor exercises if there is a stress/mixed component — these are effective first-line measures, not a delay tactic. Only if conservative measures are insufficient should MEDICATION follow — an antimuscarinic (oxybutynin/tolterodine/solifenacin, counselling anticholinergic side-effects and caution/avoidance of oxybutynin in older/frail patients) or mirabegron (a beta-3 agonist, NICE TA290; BP measured before and during treatment, contraindicated at 180/110 or more, MHRA October 2015), reviewed 4 weeks after starting, with vaginal oestrogen for postmenopausal vaginal atrophy — with referral to continence/urology services if refractory (Botox, neuromodulation). Acknowledge the significant social, sleep and quality-of-life impact and the embarrassment, take it seriously, and frame conservative management positively. The hidden agenda is the wish for a quick "pill to stop it" amid embarrassment and impact; validate the distress, exclude red flags (especially haematuria and the ovarian route → NICE NG12), and explain conservative-first with medication as a next step — not first line.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG123 (urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women, 2019) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE QS77 (urinary incontinence in women) · [3] NICE TA290 (mirabegron) · [4] MHRA Drug Safety Update, mirabegron (October 2015)
knowledge.summary: Urgency, frequency, nocturia and urge leakage suggest overactive bladder. Exclude infection, haematuria and other causes, confirm the type of incontinence, and start with a bladder diary, lifestyle change and at least 6 weeks of bladder training before medication.

points.t: NICE NG123 [1]: history to categorise stress, urgency (OAB) or mixed incontinence; urine dipstick for blood, glucose, protein, leucocytes and nitrites, with culture if infection is suspected; ask about medicines, fluid and caffeine intake. Examine in person (abdomen, pelvic examination for prolapse and atrophy, pelvic floor contraction).

NICE NG123 [1] and QS77 [2]: a bladder diary for at least 3 days, covering both working and leisure days, at initial assessment. It shows frequency, volumes, fluid and caffeine intake and leak episodes.

NICE NG12 [5]: aged 45 and over with unexplained visible haematuria without UTI, or visible haematuria that persists or recurs after successful UTI treatment → suspected cancer pathway referral (bladder and kidney). Persistent or frequent urinary urgency or frequency together with bloating, early satiety, loss of appetite or pelvic or abdominal pain is an ovarian cancer pattern in NICE NG12, but isolated urgency with a clear OAB picture does not need CA125: in women aged 40 and over with that pattern, measure CA125; at 50–59, arrange urgent direct-access pelvic and abdominal ultrasound if CA125 is 31 IU/mL or more. Ask about bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain and weight loss.

NICE NG123 [1]: recommend a trial of caffeine reduction; consider advising modification of high or low fluid intake; advise weight loss if BMI is over 30. Offer bladder training lasting for a minimum of 6 weeks as first-line treatment for urgency or mixed incontinence; supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months if there is a stress component.

NICE NG123 [1]: if bladder training is ineffective, offer an antimuscarinic after discussing benefits and adverse effects, taking account of total anticholinergic burden. Do not offer immediate-release oxybutynin to older women who may be at higher risk of sudden deterioration in physical or mental health. Review 4 weeks after starting a new OAB medicine. Mirabegron (NICE TA290 [3]) or vibegron (NICE TA999) is an option where antimuscarinics are contraindicated, ineffective or not tolerated. Doses per BNF.

MHRA DSU October 2015 [4]: mirabegron is contraindicated in severe uncontrolled hypertension (systolic 180 or more, or diastolic 110 or more); measure BP before starting and regularly during treatment.
NICE NG123 [1]: offer intravaginal oestrogen for OAB symptoms in postmenopausal women with vaginal atrophy. Systemic HRT is not a treatment for incontinence.

Refer to specialist services if OAB does not respond to conservative and drug treatment (further options include botulinum toxin A and nerve stimulation), or earlier for haematuria, a palpable bladder after voiding, suspected neurological disease, recurrent UTI or symptomatic prolapse.

model.text: Hello Mrs Foster, I’m Dr Patel. Can you hear me okay, and are you somewhere private? … Good. What can I help with today?

It’s so embarrassing. I’m bursting for the loo all the time, day and night, and sometimes I just don’t make it. I’ve started avoiding going out and I’m exhausted from getting up at night. Can you just give me a tablet to stop it? My friend takes something for hers.

Thank you for telling me. This is very common and you’re right to come; it’s clearly taking a lot out of you, stopping you going out and wrecking your sleep. I do want to help you get it under control. Can I ask some questions so we treat the right problem?
Yes, go on.
When you leak, is it that you get a sudden, desperate urge and can’t get there in time, or does it happen when you cough, sneeze or lift something?
It’s the urge. I suddenly have to go and I don’t make it. Not really when I cough.
Roughly how often do you go in the day, and how many times do you get up at night?
I’ve never counted. It feels like all the time, and I’m up more than once every night.
Have you seen any blood in your urine, or had burning or stinging when you go?
model.why: Screens NICE NG12 visible haematuria and infection

model.text: No blood, no burning.
Have you been unusually thirsty, or lost weight without trying? And any bloating, feeling full quickly, or pain low in your tummy?
model.why: Screens diabetes and NICE NG12 ovarian symptoms

model.text: Not that I’ve noticed.
Any numbness or weakness in your legs, back problems, or change in your bowels?
No, nothing like that.
What do you tend to drink through the day: tea, coffee, fizzy drinks, alcohol? And are you taking any tablets or medicines from anywhere?
Nothing unusual, I don’t think. No medicines.
You mentioned your friend’s tablet. What do you know about it, and what are you hoping it would do?
model.why: Explores the idea behind the request

model.text: Just that it stopped her rushing. I want my life back. I’m scared to go anywhere without knowing where the loo is.
That sounds really isolating. Is there anything else you’re worried this might be?
Not really. It’s more the embarrassment.

From what you describe, this sounds like an overactive bladder. The bladder muscle squeezes before it’s full, which gives that sudden urge. It’s very common and very treatable. You haven’t mentioned blood or anything worrying, which is reassuring, but I’ll still check a urine sample.
model.why: Working diagnosis in plain words; proportionate reassurance

model.text: So can I have the tablet?

Tablets are an option, and I’m not ruling them out. But the steps that work best come first, and tablets are added if those aren’t enough. The first steps often work well, and tablets can cause dry mouth, constipation and, for some, fuzziness. Would it be okay if I explain the plan?
model.why: Validates the request while explaining conservative-first

model.text: Okay.

First, a bladder diary for at least three days, including a work day and a day off if that applies: what you drink, when you go and roughly how much, and any leaks. Second, caffeine in tea, coffee and fizzy drinks irritates the bladder, so it’s worth trying decaf versions for a few weeks. And don’t cut back on fluids overall, because very concentrated urine irritates the bladder too.
model.why: NG123 diary for at least 3 days; caffeine reduction; sensible fluid intake

model.text: I could try decaf. I hadn’t thought about not cutting back.

A lot of people do cut back, so it’s worth knowing. Third, bladder training: when the urge comes, you hold on a little longer, using squeezes of your pelvic floor muscles, and gradually stretch the time between visits. It takes at least six weeks to work, so it needs patience, but most people improve. I can refer you to the continence service to support you.
model.why: NG123 bladder training for at least 6 weeks; continence service

model.text: And if it doesn’t work?

Then we add a tablet. There are two main types, and I’d go through the side effects and check your blood pressure before one of them. I’d also like you to come in for a urine test and a quick examination, to check for anything like a prolapse or dryness that we could treat directly.
model.why: Medication as next step, BP before mirabegron, in-person examination

model.text: Please let me know promptly if you see any blood in your urine, get burning or a fever, notice bloating or tummy pain that doesn’t go away, or any numbness or weakness. Can you tell me back what we’re going to do?
model.why: Specific safety-net: haematuria, infection, ovarian and neurological symptoms

model.text: Urine sample and an appointment. Three-day diary. Decaf and not cutting back fluids. Bladder training for six weeks. Tablet if that’s not enough.
Perfect. Let’s review your diary together in a few weeks. The continence service can advise on pads for now, so you can get out and about again while this starts working.
model.why: Review booked; containment products while treatment starts

model.text: Thank you. I feel less silly about it now.

social.t: Urgency often leads to avoiding outings and to broken sleep. Naming this validates her and makes the case for treatment.
Bladder symptoms are often hidden for years. An early, matter-of-fact tone makes the history easier.

legal.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): offer a chaperone for the pelvic examination and record the offer and response.

professional.t: NICE NG123: discuss the benefits and adverse effects of antimuscarinics, including anticholinergic burden, before prescribing, and review 4 weeks after starting a new medicine.
Starting an anticholinergic can add to later cognitive and falls risk; record the discussion and review regularly.

community.t: NHS continence services provide bladder training support and assessment for containment products.
Bladder Health UK and the Bladder and Bowel Community offer information and support.

redFlags: Visible haematuria at 45 or over (NICE NG12 bladder)
Persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain or urinary urgency and frequency at 40 or over (NICE NG12 ovarian: CA125)
Leg weakness, numbness or new back pain (neurological cause)
Recurrent UTI or a palpable bladder after voiding
psychosocial: Avoiding going out; fear of being caught short
Embarrassment; comparison with a friend’s treatment
ice: Idea: a tablet will stop it, as it did for her friend
Concern: embarrassment and losing her social life

playbook.diagnosis: “This sounds like an overactive bladder: the bladder muscle squeezes before it’s full, which causes that sudden urge. It’s very common and very treatable.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the bladder as a balloon with a jumpy alarm. The alarm goes off long before the balloon is full. Bladder training teaches the alarm to wait.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you’re avoiding going out and hoped for a tablet like your friend’s. I want to get your life back too. The first steps often work well, and a tablet is ready as the next step if they don’t.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the isolation and sleep loss; continence service and containment products so she can go out meanwhile.
sharedPlan: Urine dipstick (culture if infection suspected); in-person abdominal and pelvic examination with chaperone offered
Bladder diary for at least 3 days
Caffeine reduction trial; avoid restricting fluids
Bladder training for at least 6 weeks with continence service support
If ineffective: antimuscarinic (consider anticholinergic burden) or mirabegron (BP first); review 4 weeks after starting
Intravaginal oestrogen if postmenopausal with vaginal atrophy
safetyNet: Visible blood in the urine: see us promptly (NICE NG12)
Burning, fever, persistent bloating or pelvic pain, leg weakness or numbness: return
Review the diary and progress in a few weeks

pitfalls.intro: The trap is either giving the tablet on request or refusing it flatly. The marks sit in excluding red flags, conservative-first management explained well, and taking the impact seriously.

items.fail: Prescribing an antimuscarinic at the first consultation without a urine test or type of incontinence.
items.why: NG123 puts assessment, a bladder diary and bladder training first.
items.fix: Characterise urge vs stress, dip the urine, start the diary.

items.fail: Never asking about blood in the urine.
items.why: Visible haematuria at 45 or over is an NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway criterion.
items.fix: “Have you seen any blood in your urine?”

items.fail: Missing that urgency and frequency are also NICE NG12 ovarian symptoms.
items.why: At 40 or over, persistent symptoms warrant a CA125 test.
items.fix: Ask about bloating, early satiety and pelvic pain.

items.why: Concentrated urine irritates the bladder; NG123 advises modifying only high or low intake, and a caffeine reduction trial.
items.fix: “Keep drinking normally, and swap to decaf.”

items.why: Dismisses a treatable condition and her distress.
items.fix: “This is very common and very treatable, and it matters because it’s stopping you going out.”

items.why: Without the 6-week message she may stop after a week and feel it failed.
items.fix: “It takes at least six weeks. Let’s review your diary in a few weeks.”

Third, bladder training: when the urge comes, you hold on a little longer, using squeezes of your pelvic floor muscles, and gradually stretch the time between visits. It takes at least six weeks to work, so it needs patience, but most people improve. I can refer you to the continence service to support you.
SCA_MODELS.why: NG123 bladder training for at least 6 weeks; continence service

SCA_MODELS.text: And if it doesn’t work?

Then we add a tablet. There are two main types, and I’d go through the side effects and check your blood pressure before one of them. I’d also like you to come in for a urine test and a quick examination, to check for anything like a prolapse or dryness that we could treat directly.
SCA_MODELS.why: Medication as next step, BP before mirabegron, in-person examination

SCA_MODELS.text: Please let me know promptly if you see any blood in your urine, get burning or a fever, notice bloating or tummy pain that doesn’t go away, or any numbness or weakness. Can you tell me back what we’re going to do?
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net: haematuria, infection, ovarian and neurological symptoms

SCA_MODELS.text: Urine sample and an appointment. Three-day diary. Decaf and not cutting back fluids. Bladder training for six weeks. Tablet if that’s not enough.
Perfect. Let’s review your diary together in a few weeks. The continence service can advise on pads for now, so you can get out and about again while this starts working.
SCA_MODELS.why: Review booked; containment products while treatment starts

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you. I feel less silly about it now.

SCA_STEM.name: Diane Foster
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: No previous consultations for urinary symptoms.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation: urgency, frequency day and night and occasional leaking; asking for a tablet to stop it.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG123 (urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women, 2019) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE QS77 (urinary incontinence in women) · [3] NICE TA290 (mirabegron) · [4] MHRA Drug Safety Update, mirabegron (October 2015)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Urgency, frequency, nocturia and urge leakage suggest overactive bladder. Exclude infection, haematuria and other causes, confirm the type of incontinence, and start with a bladder diary, lifestyle change and at least 6 weeks of bladder training before medication.

points.t: NICE NG123 [1]: history to categorise stress, urgency (OAB) or mixed incontinence; urine dipstick for blood, glucose, protein, leucocytes and nitrites, with culture if infection is suspected; ask about medicines, fluid and caffeine intake. Examine in person (abdomen, pelvic examination for prolapse and atrophy, pelvic floor contraction).

NICE NG123 [1] and QS77 [2]: a bladder diary for at least 3 days, covering both working and leisure days, at initial assessment. It shows frequency, volumes, fluid and caffeine intake and leak episodes.

NICE NG12 [5]: aged 45 and over with unexplained visible haematuria without UTI, or visible haematuria that persists or recurs after successful UTI treatment → suspected cancer pathway referral (bladder and kidney). Persistent or frequent urinary urgency or frequency together with bloating, early satiety, loss of appetite or pelvic or abdominal pain is an ovarian cancer pattern in NICE NG12, but isolated urgency with a clear OAB picture does not need CA125: in women aged 40 and over with that pattern, measure CA125; at 50–59, arrange urgent direct-access pelvic and abdominal ultrasound if CA125 is 31 IU/mL or more. Ask about bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain and weight loss.

NICE NG123 [1]: recommend a trial of caffeine reduction; consider advising modification of high or low fluid intake; advise weight loss if BMI is over 30. Offer bladder training lasting for a minimum of 6 weeks as first-line treatment for urgency or mixed incontinence; supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months if there is a stress component.

NICE NG123 [1]: if bladder training is ineffective, offer an antimuscarinic after discussing benefits and adverse effects, taking account of total anticholinergic burden. Do not offer immediate-release oxybutynin to older women who may be at higher risk of sudden deterioration in physical or mental health. Review 4 weeks after starting a new OAB medicine. Mirabegron (NICE TA290 [3]) or vibegron (NICE TA999) is an option where antimuscarinics are contraindicated, ineffective or not tolerated. Doses per BNF.

MHRA DSU October 2015 [4]: mirabegron is contraindicated in severe uncontrolled hypertension (systolic 180 or more, or diastolic 110 or more); measure BP before starting and regularly during treatment.
NICE NG123 [1]: offer intravaginal oestrogen for OAB symptoms in postmenopausal women with vaginal atrophy. Systemic HRT is not a treatment for incontinence.

Refer to specialist services if OAB does not respond to conservative and drug treatment (further options include botulinum toxin A and nerve stimulation), or earlier for haematuria, a palpable bladder after voiding, suspected neurological disease, recurrent UTI or symptomatic prolapse.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked privacy; open question; let her describe urgency, leakage and the impact on going out and sleep.
Social withdrawal, embarrassment and exhaustion from nocturia explored.
Picked up “avoiding going out” and “my friend takes something” and used both.
Idea (a tablet will stop it, like her friend), concern (embarrassment, being caught short), expectation (a prescription today).
Urine dipstick and culture if indicated; in-person abdominal and pelvic examination; bladder diary for at least 3 days.
OAB vs stress or mixed incontinence, UTI, diabetes, neurological causes, medicines, caffeine and fluid habits.
Screened visible haematuria (NICE NG12 bladder at 45+), NICE NG12 ovarian symptoms, diabetes and neurological red flags.
Urgency-predominant incontinence consistent with overactive bladder.
Caffeine reduction, fluid advice, bladder training for at least 6 weeks, continence service; antimuscarinic or mirabegron as the next step.
Advice not to restrict fluids; anticholinergic burden and BP considered before medication; containment products meanwhile.
Clear return triggers (haematuria, infection, bloating or pain, neurology); diary review booked.

social.t: Urgency often leads to avoiding outings and to broken sleep. Naming this validates her and makes the case for treatment.
Bladder symptoms are often hidden for years. An early, matter-of-fact tone makes the history easier.

legal.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): offer a chaperone for the pelvic examination and record the offer and response.

professional.t: NICE NG123: discuss the benefits and adverse effects of antimuscarinics, including anticholinergic burden, before prescribing, and review 4 weeks after starting a new medicine.
Starting an anticholinergic can add to later cognitive and falls risk; record the discussion and review regularly.

community.t: NHS continence services provide bladder training support and assessment for containment products.
Bladder Health UK and the Bladder and Bowel Community offer information and support.

redFlags: Visible haematuria at 45 or over (NICE NG12 bladder)
Persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain or urinary urgency and frequency at 40 or over (NICE NG12 ovarian: CA125)
Leg weakness, numbness or new back pain (neurological cause)
Recurrent UTI or a palpable bladder after voiding
psychosocial: Avoiding going out; fear of being caught short
Embarrassment; comparison with a friend’s treatment
ice: Idea: a tablet will stop it, as it did for her friend
Concern: embarrassment and losing her social life

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This sounds like an overactive bladder: the bladder muscle squeezes before it’s full, which causes that sudden urge. It’s very common and very treatable.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the bladder as a balloon with a jumpy alarm. The alarm goes off long before the balloon is full. Bladder training teaches the alarm to wait.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you’re avoiding going out and hoped for a tablet like your friend’s. I want to get your life back too. The first steps often work well, and a tablet is ready as the next step if they don’t.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the isolation and sleep loss; continence service and containment products so she can go out meanwhile.
sharedPlan: Urine dipstick (culture if infection suspected); in-person abdominal and pelvic examination with chaperone offered
Bladder diary for at least 3 days
Caffeine reduction trial; avoid restricting fluids
Bladder training for at least 6 weeks with continence service support
If ineffective: antimuscarinic (consider anticholinergic burden) or mirabegron (BP first); review 4 weeks after starting
Intravaginal oestrogen if postmenopausal with vaginal atrophy
safetyNet: Visible blood in the urine: see us promptly (NICE NG12)
Burning, fever, persistent bloating or pelvic pain, leg weakness or numbness: return
Review the diary and progress in a few weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is either giving the tablet on request or refusing it flatly. The marks sit in excluding red flags, conservative-first management explained well, and taking the impact seriously.

items.fail: Prescribing an antimuscarinic at the first consultation without a urine test or type of incontinence.
items.why: NG123 puts assessment, a bladder diary and bladder training first.
items.fix: Characterise urge vs stress, dip the urine, start the diary.

items.fail: Never asking about blood in the urine.
items.why: Visible haematuria at 45 or over is an NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway criterion.
items.fix: “Have you seen any blood in your urine?”

items.fail: Missing that urgency and frequency are also NICE NG12 ovarian symptoms.
items.why: At 40 or over, persistent symptoms warrant a CA125 test.
items.fix: Ask about bloating, early satiety and pelvic pain.

items.why: Concentrated urine irritates the bladder; NG123 advises modifying only high or low intake, and a caffeine reduction trial.
items.fix: “Keep drinking normally, and swap to decaf.”

items.why: Dismisses a treatable condition and her distress.
items.fix: “This is very common and very treatable, and it matters because it’s stopping you going out.”

items.why: Without the 6-week message she may stop after a week and feel it failed.
items.fix: “It takes at least six weeks. Let’s review your diary in a few weeks.”
